Wrest

REST -- from Old English wraestan ('to twist, wrench'); the same Germanic root behind wrestle. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To wrest is to forcefully take something away from someone's grasp or control.

Corporate raiders spent months trying to wrest control of the family-owned company through a hostile takeover.

Worked Example

After years of backroom deals, the junior senator finally managed to wrest control of the committee away from its longtime chairman.

That forceful, often difficult act of taking something away from someone who is holding onto it tightly -- whether a physical object or a position of power -- is exactly what it means to wrest something.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wrench: to pull or twist something suddenly and violently

seize: to take hold of something forcefully or suddenly

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

surrender: to give up control or possession of something

relinquish: to formally give up a right or possession

Where it sits · how forcefully it is taken — wrench → wrest → seize

wrench vs. wrest: He wrenched the stuck drawer open with a loud crack.

seize vs. wrest: Soldiers seized the bridge before the enemy could reach it.

Put it together

Put it together: Wrest comes from Old English wraestan, 'to twist or wrench' -- the very same Germanic root behind wrestle, which describes the physical twisting and grappling of a struggle for control.

Word Choice

Wrest almost always implies real resistance -- you wrest something away from someone who is actively holding on, unlike simply taking or receiving something freely offered.
